newsitem.title: USA: U.S. revokes visa of Cambodian tycoon.
newsitem.headline: U.S. revokes visa of Cambodian tycoon.

text.p: The United States said on Thursday it would revoke the visa of Teng Bunma, a wealthy Cambodian tycoon who is alleged to be involved in drug trafficking and reportedly helped finance last month's coup.
"We have decided that based on information we have, we will revoke his visa," State Department spokesman James Rubin told a news briefing.
"If the formal request comes from our embassy in Phnom Penh, we will not allow him to travel to the United States," he said.

Rubin described Teng Bunma as a "prominent businessman who we believe -- there is reliable reporting -- has been involved in drug trafficking. And we take the possible drug trafficking of this kind very, very seriously."

He quoted Teng Bunma as saying "his support for (Cambodian strongman) Hun Sen assisted an effort and events that we (United States) have condemned quite strongly," namely the bloody coup by which Second Prime Minister Hun Sen ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh.

"We certainly would condemn any individual's involvement in, or financial backing for, the events that occurred in Phnom Penh some weeks ago because it was bad news for the people of Cambodia. It was bad news for democracy in Cambodia," Rubin said.

"And the fact that a drug trafficker is claiming to have these connections is a major problem for us ... So the combination of the reliable reports on drug trafficking has made us decide to revoke his visa," he said.
Cambodia has a major drug trafficking problem and the United States will continue to urge the government to try to solve the problem, he said.
The United States, despite condemning the coup and delaying $60 million in aid to the government in response, is working with the government in other ways.

This week, Washington granted Phnom Penh duty-free status on more than 6,000 items under the U.S. generalized system of preferences program, which allows Cambodia to import those items free of duty to the United States.
Asked why this decision does not undercut the message sent by halting aid, Rubin said, "There is a difference between assistance to a government and trade."
"This is a (trade) preference that is linked to their labor laws and how they treat their workers and making sure that some commerce can grow there," he said.
Rubin stressed that "we're trying to not harm the Cambodian people ... They've suffered from genocide, and they've suffered from the loss of democracy."
"We think that a preference like this that encourages better labor treatment for the people who actually have to do the work is appropriate, given that general policy framework."
